projection.statement: Assess whether the main claims are supported by accurate, convincing, and clearly presented evidence; additional evidence or narrower claims are both legitimate closure routes.
Assess whether some individuals in TMLR's audience would be interested in the findings; do not substitute novelty, state-of-the-art performance, or predicted impact as independent acceptance gates.

sections.extracted_fact: TMLR acceptance asks whether claims have accurate, convincing and clear support and whether some readers would find the findings interesting.

verbatim_excerpts.text: Are the claims made in the submission supported by accurate, convincing and clear evidence?

verbatim_excerpts.source_locator: Acceptance Criteria > first question > additional evidence route
verbatim_excerpts.text: Often, this will lead reviewers to ask the authors to provide more evidence by running more experiments.

verbatim_excerpts.source_locator: Acceptance Criteria > first question > closure options
verbatim_excerpts.text: Another is simply for the authors to adjust (reduce) their claims.
Would some individuals in TMLR's audience be interested in the findings of this paper?

verbatim_excerpts.source_locator: Acceptance Criteria > second question > significance and SOTA are not gates
verbatim_excerpts.text: Crucially, it should not be used as a reason to reject work that isn't considered “significant” or “impactful” because it isn't achieving a new state-of-the-art on some benchmark.

verbatim_excerpts.source_locator: Acceptance Criteria > second question > novelty is not a gate
verbatim_excerpts.text: Nor should it form the basis for rejecting work on a method considered not “novel enough”, as novelty of the studied method is not a necessary criteria for acceptance.

verbatim_excerpts.source_locator: Acceptance Criteria > second question > significance and impact certifications
verbatim_excerpts.text: TMLR instead relies on certifications (such as “Featured” and “Outstanding”) to provide annotations on submissions that pertain to (more speculative) assertions on significance or potential for impact.
